note: First-pass dataset. Rarity tiers and regional ranges need review by a Kruger guide before launch — see docs/SPEC.md.

species.description: Widespread but almost never seen. Digs the burrows that warthog, porcupine and hyena later occupy — an entire ecosystem depends on it.
species.habitat: Woodland and grassland with termite mounds
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late on a night drive, well after dark

species.description: A hyena that eats nothing but harvester termites — up to 300,000 in a night. Looks like a slender striped hyena with a raised mane.
Blotched and heavy-set with a raised black crest along the spine. Marks territory with communal latrines called civetries.
Kruger holds well over ten thousand. Breeding herds are led by the oldest female, who carries the memory of where water is in a drought.
species.habitat: Everywhere, concentrating near rivers in the dry season

species.description: Perhaps 300 in the whole park. Packs cover huge distances daily, so a sighting is genuine luck rather than knowledge.
The ancestor of every domestic cat. Told apart by rich rufous behind the ears and much longer legs than a housecat.
Moves in noisy packs of twenty or more, constantly chattering to stay in contact while foraging through leaf litter.
Enormous ears used to listen for termites underground. Common in the Kalahari but genuinely scarce in Kruger's open northern grassland.
A browser with a hooked prehensile lip, smaller and far more aggressive than the white rhino. Critically endangered and rarely seen.
Pairs bond for life and hold a territory together. The rising, wavering call at dusk is one of the definitive sounds of the bushveld.
Densest on the southern and central grasslands. Calving is tightly synchronised in the wet season, flooding predators with more prey than they can take.
A handful of records in the entire park, all in the far north. Shaggy, long-haired and solitary, unlike the spotted hyena in every way.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Deep night, far north — essentially chance

species.description: Solitary and shy, sticking tight to cover. A sharp barking alarm call is usually the only sign one is there.
Nocturnal, hairy and bad-tempered — everything the warthog is not. Sounders keep to dense cover and are seldom seen in daylight.
Herds run to several hundred. Old solitary bulls — dagha boys — are unpredictable and account for the species' reputation.
species.habitat: Grassland and woodland near permanent water

species.description: Africa's largest rodent. Charges backwards to drive quills into an attacker; they detach easily and cannot be shot out, despite the myth.
species.habitat: Widespread; shelters in caves and burrows

species.description: Black-tufted ears and enough vertical leap to take birds out of the air. Secretive and very seldom seen in daylight.
Troops of up to a hundred, rigidly hierarchical. Never leave a car window open near them — they have learned exactly what a cooler box is.
species.habitat: Everywhere, especially near camps and koppies
species.bestTimeToSpot: Daylight — roosts in trees at night

species.description: Needs open ground to run and loses kills constantly to lion and hyena, which keeps numbers low. Favours the central grasslands.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Mid-morning — hunts later than other cats

species.description: Named for its diving run into cover. The only small antelope in the park that regularly eats meat when it gets the chance.
species.habitat: Bush and woodland with good cover

species.description: The largest antelope on earth, and shy out of proportion to its size. Tendons in the legs click audibly as the herd walks.
Africa's smallest carnivore. Lives inside termite mounds and posts a sentry on top while the rest of the group feeds.
Browses above the reach of every other herbivore. Watch for the splayed-leg stance at water, the only moment it is genuinely vulnerable.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time — visible from a distance

species.description: Bulls carry spiralled horns over a metre long. Despite the size they vanish into thick bush the moment they stop moving.
The most trafficked mammal on earth and the sighting of a lifetime. Rolls into an armoured ball when threatened — which is exactly why poachers can simply pick it up.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Night drives — a handful of sightings a year

species.description: Spends the day submerged and grazes on land at night, walking many kilometres from water. Kills more people in Africa than any other large mammal.
Loose, thick skin lets it twist round inside its own hide when grabbed. Will drive lions off a kill through sheer refusal to leave.
species.habitat: Widespread; mostly nocturnal but active at dusk

species.description: The most abundant antelope in the park and the staple prey of almost every predator in it. Herds scatter in explosive leaps when alarmed.
species.habitat: Open woodland and the edges of riverine bush
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time of day, year round

species.description: Stands on the very tips of cylindrical hooves and is found nowhere but rock. Pairs are near-inseparable, one always watching while the other feeds.
Cat-like but not a cat. Habituated individuals patrol the rafters of several rest camps after dark.
species.bestTimeToSpot: After dark in camp, or on night drives

species.description: Solitary, largely nocturnal, and hauls kills into trees to keep them from hyena. The hardest of the Big Five to find on your own.
species.habitat: Riverine bush, drainage lines and rocky ground
species.bestTimeToSpot: First and last light, on riverine roads

species.description: Tiny, huge-eyed, and capable of leaping several metres between branches. Eyeshine in a torch beam is usually the first clue.
Sleeps up to twenty hours a day, which is why most sightings are of a flat cat under a bush. Prides are held by coalitions of related males.
species.habitat: Open woodland and grassland near prey concentrations

species.description: Confined to a handful of rocky hillsides in the north of the park. Small, grey and easily mistaken for a common reedbuck at distance.
Males and females look like different species entirely — shaggy slate-grey bulls, bright chestnut ewes. Strongly tied to dense riverine bush.
Almost always found alongside wildebeest, which benefit from the zebra's better eyesight while the zebra benefits from their numbers.
One of the rarest large antelope in Kruger, down to a few dozen animals in the far northern sandveld. A genuine trophy sighting.
Jet-black bulls with scimitar horns swept back over the shoulders. Kruger's population is small and concentrated in the north.
Lies up motionless all day and bolts only at the last second. The standard opening sighting on any night drive.
Long-legged and huge-eared, hunting rodents by sound alone in long grass and pouncing vertically. Tied to wetland margins.
species.habitat: Tall grass and reedbeds near water
species.bestTimeToSpot: Dawn and dusk in marshy areas

species.description: Small, grizzled and almost entirely nocturnal, which is why it is so rarely recorded despite being reasonably common.
Solitary and quick, identified by the black tail tip it flicks upward as it runs across a road.
Bound away with a shrill whistle and a distinctive rocking-horse gait, flashing the white underside of the tail.
species.habitat: Tall grass and reedbeds near water
species.bestTimeToSpot: Dawn and dusk in wetland areas

species.description: A capable hunter, not merely a scavenger — clans kill more than they steal. Females are larger and outrank every male.
species.habitat: Widespread; dens in culverts and drainage lines
species.bestTimeToSpot: Just after gate opening or before closing

species.description: A small, rufous antelope seen alone or in pairs. Freezes flat in the grass when threatened rather than running.
One of the smallest antelope in Africa, standing barely 35cm. In Kruger it is restricted to the sand forest of the Pafuri region.
species.habitat: Dense sand forest and thicket in the far north

species.description: Far larger than the lesser bushbaby, with a wailing call that sounds unnervingly like a child. Restricted to tall riverine forest.
species.habitat: Riverine forest, especially in the north

species.description: Also called the mopane squirrel. Flicks its tail and scolds loudly from a trunk, spiralling round to keep the wood between you and it.
The fastest antelope in southern Africa. Rare in Kruger and largely confined to the northern grasslands.
Uses distinct alarm calls for leopard, eagle and snake, and other species listen in. A rare case of a genuine animal vocabulary.
Runs with its tail held vertical like a flag. Reverses into abandoned aardvark burrows to sleep so it can face any intruder.
species.habitat: Open grassland and around rest camps

species.description: Marked with a white ring on the rump that looks like it sat on a freshly painted toilet seat. Never strays far from permanent water.
species.habitat: Riverine grassland within a few kilometres of water

species.description: A grazer with a broad square lip — the name is a corruption of the Dutch for wide, not a colour. Concentrated in the south.
The largest mongoose in Africa, and strictly nocturnal. The bushy white tail catches a spotlight from a long way off.
The ringing call thrown back over its shoulder is the sound most people associate with African water, whether or not they know the bird.
Rocks side to side in flight like a tightrope walker, which is what the French name means. Almost no visible tail.
species.habitat: Open savanna, hunting on the wing

species.description: Among the heaviest flying birds on earth. Displaying males inflate the throat into a startling white balloon.
The largest vulture in Africa and dominant at a carcass — its bill opens hides the others cannot. Bare pink head and heavy folds of skin.
species.habitat: Open savanna; nests in flat-topped trees

species.description: The most photographed bird in the park. Named for the tumbling aerial roll males perform in display flight.
species.habitat: Open woodland, perched on dead branches and posts

species.description: Africa's largest eagle, powerful enough to take a young impala. Territories are enormous, so sightings are widely spaced.
species.habitat: Open savanna; perches on tall dead trees

species.description: A huge ginger owl that hunts fish by touch from a low branch. In Kruger it is essentially a Luvuvhu River bird and the hardest of the Big Six.
species.habitat: Tall riverine forest along the Luvuvhu

species.description: Fewer than thirty breeding pairs in the whole park. Females have yellow eyes, males brown — one of the easier sexes to call in the field.
Turkey-sized, walks rather than flies, and booms at dawn like a distant lion. Groups raise one chick every nine years or so.
Africa's largest owl, identified instantly by pink eyelids it shows when blinking. Roosts in big riverine trees by day.
species.habitat: Large trees along rivers and drainage lines
species.bestTimeToSpot: Dusk, or roosting by day if you know the tree

species.description: The commonest vulture at a kill, and collapsing fast across its range through poisoning. Circling birds are the best kill-finder in the park.
species.habitat: Open woodland; nests in tall trees
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late morning, circling or at a carcass

species.description: Named for the ink-black mouth, not the body, which is gunmetal grey. Fast, alert, and far more inclined to flee than to engage.
species.habitat: Woodland, termite mounds and rocky ground
species.bestTimeToSpot: Warm mornings — observe from the vehicle only

species.description: The largest tortoise in the park and the only one that cannot pull its head straight back — it folds the neck sideways.
Large individuals in the Olifants and Luvuvhu exceed four metres. Basks with its mouth open to shed heat, not as a threat.
Africa's largest snake, reaching five metres. Females coil around the eggs and stay with the hatchlings, unusual among snakes.
species.habitat: Riverine bush, rocky outcrops and dense cover

species.description: Africa's largest lizard, up to two metres. Raids crocodile nests and swims with the tail alone, legs held flat against the body.
Not a shrew and not related to elephants — its closest living relatives are elephants, aardvarks and hyraxes. Bolts between rocks on fixed, swept trails it keeps clear of leaf litter.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning on rocks, before the heat

species.description: Builds the untidy stick tenements that hang off the western side of tall trees and windmills. Easy to see and almost never looked at, which is the joke of the Small Five.
species.habitat: Open woodland, usually near large trees and camps
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, around camps and picnic sites

species.description: The conical pits in soft sand at every picnic site are its traps. The larva waits buried at the bottom and flicks sand at anything that slides in. The adult, pictured, looks like a slender dragonfly and comes to lights at night. Several species dig the pits, so the Small Five counts them together.
species.habitat: Fine dry sand under trees, out of the rain
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any picnic site — look down before you look up

species.description: Can carry many times its own weight, and the males fight with the horn. Turns up at camp lights on humid summer nights, which is very nearly the only time anyone sees one.
species.habitat: Woodland; larvae develop in rotting wood and dung
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer nights, at camp lights after rain

species.description: The largest bird alive, and the fastest thing on two legs. Localised in Kruger to the open southern and central grasslands, so it is a sighting you drive to rather than one that finds you.
species.habitat: Open short grassland and sparse savanna

species.description: An eagle that walks. Strides through grassland stamping on snakes with enough force to kill them outright, and roosts in a flat-topped acacia at dusk. Numbers have fallen sharply across its range.
species.habitat: Open grassland and lightly wooded savanna
species.bestTimeToSpot: Walking open ground in the morning

species.description: Not a goose but a shelduck, and the loudest thing at any waterhole. Pairs bond for life and will see off animals many times their size to defend a nest.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, at the water's edge
